summary: Specifies a middle-ground way for the IETF to run experiments on its own process. Earlier process changes were either announced informally by the IESG, which was too lightweight, or made through the full protocol specification mechanism, which was too heavyweight.

eli5.summary: Before changing the rules of a game for everyone, a group tries the new rule for a while, tells everybody it is a trial, and then decides if it worked.

questions: how does the ietf try new processes
what is an ietf process experiment
what is a sunset in an ietf experiment
how long is an ietf last call
subtitle: How the IETF can try out a change to its own rules for a limited time before making it permanent.

tldr.problem: The IETF changed its process in two ways. Informal IESG announcements were too lightweight and sometimes out of step with the community, while the full standards process was too heavyweight for untried ideas.
tldr.mechanism: A proposed change is written up as an Internet-Draft with a sunset date, goes through a four-week IETF Last Call, and is then published as an Experimental RFC and tried out.
tldr.outcome: At or before the sunset the IESG either revises the document into a BCP RFC based on operational experience or lets the procedure expire.

facts.label: Sunset timeout
facts.value: Typically not more than one year after adoption

today: RFC 3933 is a Best Current Practice published in November 2004, and the metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Middle Ground for Process Change
sections.content:
RFC 3933 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 93) about how the IETF changes itself, not about a network protocol. It specifies a middle-ground approach that relies on a model of proposing and carrying out an experiment, evaluating it, and then establishing permanent procedures based on operational experience.

The abstract describes the problem it fixes: earlier process changes were made either by announcement from the IESG, sometimes with limited community involvement, or through the same mechanism used for protocol specification. The first often proved too lightweight, the second too heavyweight.
sections.eli5: A club wants to try a new rule but does not want to argue for months first. This RFC says: try it for a short time, then decide.

sections.title: The Two Older Mechanisms
sections.content:
Since the 1992 changes documented in RFC 1396, the IETF has used two mechanisms for process changes.

  • The IESG adopted procedural changes on its own initiative and documented them informally, using the wide discretion implicitly granted to it by RFC 2026. This was a lightweight route, but there was sometimes too little alignment with the larger IETF community.
  • The RFC 2026 standards process was used to find a community of interest, hold BoFs, charter a working group and build IETF-wide consensus, usually ending in a BCP. This gave full community involvement but little flexibility.

The RFC notes that the IETF does not change its formal processes often. It cites the IPR clarifications in RFC 3667 and RFC 3668 as the first documented changes to RFC 2026 since 1996, and says the community is understandably reluctant to make permanent changes with untried procedures.
sections.eli5: One way to change the rules was quick but not everyone heard about it. The other way involved everybody but took forever. Neither was great for testing a new idea.

sections.title: The Process Experiment Procedure
sections.content:
The RFC regularizes and formalizes the informal IESG mechanism and permits and encourages the IESG to adopt process experiments in four steps.

  1. An Internet-Draft describes the proposed new or altered procedure. A problem statement and specific evaluation criteria are desirable but not required, to keep the requirements lightweight. The draft must state an explicit sunset timeout, typically not to exceed one year after adoption.
  2. If the IESG thinks the proposal is plausible and plausibly useful, a four-week IETF Last Call is started. The IESG may set up its own way of screening proposals, such as requiring endorsements, but review steps that cause significant delays are outside the intent of the specification.
  3. After the Last Call the IESG reevaluates the proposal. If it is appropriate, a second Internet-Draft is produced that cleans up definitional issues and responds to issues raised in the Last Call.
  4. The document and experiment are announced, the experiment begins, and the document is forwarded for publication as an Experimental RFC.

The RFC is deliberately vague about where the drafts come from: a working group, design team, individual, editing group or the IESG itself may write them.
sections.eli5: Write down the idea and an end date, let everyone comment for four weeks, fix the write-up, then announce it and start the trial.

sections.title: Scope, Consensus and Abandoning an Experiment
sections.content:
The IESG may use this mechanism, based on Experimental RFCs, to gain experience with proposed changes to BCP specifications. No BCP needs to be approved for an experiment until it is found to have value.

The IESG can reach a conclusion that an idea is bad at any stage and abandon the experiment. It may recommend publishing the experimental document with a discussion of why it was a bad idea, but is not required to.

An experiment does not have to apply to the whole IETF. A proposal may select areas, working groups, or working groups meeting some criterion, such as those created after a particular time or of a specified age.

The IESG's decision to go ahead or not is expected to reflect its judgment of rough consensus in the community. That judgment may be appealed using the usual procedures, but the RFC reminds everyone that trying something for a fixed period is typically a better engineering approach than extended philosophical discussion without experience.
sections.eli5: The group can stop the trial at any time if it is a bad idea, and the trial can be run with just a few classes instead of the whole school.

sections.title: How an Experiment Ends
sections.content:
At or before the sunset timeout, the IESG either revises, or causes to be revised, the document into a BCP RFC, or the procedure expires and presumably is not tried again unless something changes radically. If it becomes a BCP, that BCP reflects what the authors call operational experience in the real world.

A document explaining why the experiment succeeded or failed would be desirable, but the RFC says it could not realistically be a requirement.

The RFC also notes that if the procedures and procedural exceptions the IESG has adopted over the last decade are legitimate, then the IESG has the authority to institute these changes by bootstrapping this process.
sections.eli5: When the trial time is up, the rule either becomes a real rule or quietly goes away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it specifies a mechanism for evolving IETF procedures and does not raise or consider any protocol-specific security issues. It does ask the IESG to take care that process experiments do not reduce the quality of security review and consideration for protocols, or at least that proposals contain early detection and correction mechanisms should quality deteriorate.
sections.eli5: When trying a new rule, make sure it does not make the safety checks worse, and have a way to notice if it does.

messages.label: I-D with sunset
messages.note: Describes the new or altered procedure and states an explicit sunset.

messages.label: Four-week Last Call
messages.note: Started if the proposal is plausible and plausibly useful.

messages.label: Last Call comments
messages.note: The IESG reevaluates the proposal afterwards.

messages.label: Announce and start
messages.note: A second I-D is forwarded for publication as an Experimental RFC.
